newsitem.title: JORDAN: Shooting revealed Jordan's uneasy peace with Israel.
newsitem.headline: Shooting revealed Jordan's uneasy peace with Israel.

text.p: Jordanian army private Ahmed Daqamsa, sentenced on Saturday to hard labour for life for gunning down seven Israeli schoolgirls, laid bare the deep divisions in Jordan over its peace accord with Israel.
He was damned by champions of the 1994 treaty with the Jewish state and hailed as a hero by its opponents after he shot the girls on a school outing in March.
King Hussein, who has tried to sell the peace deal to a sceptical public, said Daqamsa should have been shot dead on the spot by his comrades.
"It is a mark of shame on all who were directly responsible for the perpetrator, and all who saw him in his act and did not kill him immediately," he said in a public letter to the army.
"We do not betray people with whom we have made peace."
But not all Jordanians shared the king's outrage.
"Any military man would have acted in the same way," said member of parliament Toujan Feisal, a fierce critic of the peace deal. "He was a soldier who was acting against occupiers."

Military prosecutors portrayed Daqamsa, an army driver with a record of mental problems, as a scheming, deviant assassin. Defence lawyers said he was a troubled but pious patriot who was teased by the girls, aged 11 to 13, while he prayed.
Whatever his motives, Daqamsa became a symbol of rejection of the peace accord.
"He stands for the conscience of the Jordanian people. People in Jordan do not like Jews," Islamist member of parliament Bassam al-Amoush said in a recent interview.

Unease at the peace treaty has been fuelled in Jordan by the absence of material benefits promised from the accord, and by the stalemate in Palestinian self-rule talks since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu came to power last year.
Inside the court, Daqamsa's supporters included parliamentary deputies, a prominent union leader and a former prime minister.
For the prosecution, Israeli witnesses gave evidence in a Jordanian court for the first time.
Defence lawyers objected and tried to rule their testimony inadmissable. King Hussein welcomed them publicly to a dinner he was attending with hundreds of his top military officers.
The site of the shooting, a patch of borderland returned to Jordan under the peace accord and then leased back to Israel, is symbolic for both sides.

The government says the area was "liberated" by the treaty but the opposition say that by leasing the land back, Jordan had meekly surrendered territory to a country it had been formally at war with for 46 years.
"This is still occupied land," said Amoush. "I cannot drive there in my car, but Israelis are free to go there."

"We all know this land has not been liberated," Feisal said after the verdict. "This was a political trial right from the beginning. They wanted him executed but they did not dare issue that verdict because the Jordanians would have reacted very violently."
Israel said the verdict was "eminently justified".
But Feisal said the outside world was more concerned by a handful of Israeli victims than hundreds of Arabs killed in Lebanon or the West Bank in recent years.
"The Israeli atrocities are unimaginable. They have exceeded the Nazis and everyone is turning a blind eye to it, which is really aggravating the Jordanian people," she said.

One opposition newspaper published on its front page this month a picture of Daqamsa next to the face of former Israeli prime minister Shimon Peres, super-imposed on a picture of Lebanese victims of Israeli shellings last year.
"Who's the terrorist?" the paper asked.
For King Hussein, it was not just his peace with Israel which was jolted by the shooting. He said Daqamsa had also dealt a blow to Jordan's armed forces.
Diplomats say a number of officers in the northern region around Baqoura where the shooting occurred have been suspended.

They said the army was investigating how a soldier with a record of mental disturbance and military disobedience came to be stationed on a sensitive border site and, according to military prosecutors, was issued at his request with more than 200 rounds of ammunition.
